reconcile.connective: Commentators dissolve the tenfold gap two ways — a 'stall' in Kings counting ten horses to one Chronicles stable, or 'forty thousand' as an old copyist's error for 'four thousand.'

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, who curates the contradiction at its source, presses the two figures at face value: one book says forty thousand stalls, the other four thousand, a difference of a factor of ten about the same king.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "How many stalls did Solomon have?"
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "How many stalls did Solomon have?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/stalls.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It has been conjectured [GESENIUS, Hebrew Lexicon] that the original term may signify not only stall or stable, but a number of horses occupying the same number of stalls. Supposing that ten were put together in one part, this would make forty thousand.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB names the exact 40,000-vs-4,000 gap and gives the leading harmonization: a 'stall' in Kings = ten horses per Chronicles stall, reconciling the tenfold difference.

excerpts.excerpt_text: That is, ten horses in every stable, which in all amounts to forty thousand, as 1 Kings 4:26.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A compact second voice stating the same ten-per-stall harmonization and explicitly cross-referencing 1 Kings 4:26 to make the two figures one.

excerpts.excerpt_text: From this collation of parallel places we may rest satisfied that there is a corruption in the numbers somewhere; and as a sort of medium, we may take for the whole four thousand stalls, one thousand four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke collates Kings, Chronicles, LXX, Syriac and the Targum and resolves the gap textually, taking 4,000 stalls as the true number — the copyist-error wing of the harmonization.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on 1 Kings 4:26
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this exact pair directly, collating 1 Kings 4:26, 2 Chronicles 9:25, 10:26 and the versions to argue the 40,000 figure reflects a numerical corruption and 4,000 is the original.

link.title: Defending Inerrancy: 1 Kings 4:26 — How can this verse say Solomon had 40,000 stalls when 2 Chronicles 9:25 says he had only 4,000 stalls?
